items.prompt: What is usability testing, most precisely?
choices: Asking people whether they like how a design looks
Watching real people attempt real tasks on a design, unaided, and observing what happens
A focus group discussion about a product's features
A team review meeting where designers critique each other's mockups
items.explanation: Usability testing is about observed behavior on real tasks, not stated opinion. Liking how something looks, discussing features in a group, and internal design critique are all different activities that don't tell you whether a first-time user can actually complete a task.
items.reference:
🎯 Give a task, not a question
👀 Watch what they do, not what they say they'd do
🚫 Not a survey, not a focus group

Why: stated opinion and observed behavior reliably diverge — testing measures the second one.

items.prompt: A team runs a session where they ask users 'On a scale of 1-5, how easy was this to use?' after showing them the screens without giving them a task. Is this usability testing?
choices: Yes, any structured session with real users counts
No — there's no task being attempted and no behavior being observed, only a rating being collected
Yes, as long as at least 5 people rate it
No, because ratings can never be part of usability testing
items.explanation: The defining feature of usability testing is a real task attempted, with behavior observed. A rating collected with no task attached is closer to a survey — it measures impression, not whether the design actually works for a concrete goal.
items.reference:
🎯 Give a task, not a question
👀 Watch what they do, not what they say they'd do
🚫 Not a survey, not a focus group

Why: stated opinion and observed behavior reliably diverge — testing measures the second one.

items.prompt: Why can't a design team reliably evaluate their own design's usability just by looking at it together?
choices: Because teams are always biased toward liking their own work
Because they already know what every label and icon is supposed to mean, which makes it impossible to experience it the way a first-time user does
Because design reviews are always too short to catch problems
Because only paying customers' opinions count
items.explanation: This is the curse of knowledge: once you know what something means, you can't easily imagine not knowing it. It's not simple bias or liking your own work — it's that the team's prior knowledge itself removes the exact confusion a first-time user would experience.
items.reference:
🎯 Give a task, not a question
👀 Watch what they do, not what they say they'd do
🚫 Not a survey, not a focus group

Why: stated opinion and observed behavior reliably diverge — testing measures the second one.

items.prompt: What does 'task success rate' measure?
choices: The percentage of participants who said they enjoyed the task
The percentage of participants who completed a specific task correctly, without being rescued or helped
How fast the fastest participant finished a task
The number of tasks a design has in total
items.explanation: Task success rate is completions-without-help divided by attempts, for one specific task. It says nothing about speed or enjoyment on its own — those are separate metrics a team might also track.
items.reference:
✅ Finished unaided = success
❌ Gave up or got help = failure
🔢 Rate = successes ÷ attempts, per task

Why: it's computed per task, not once for the whole product.

items.prompt: Out of 8 participants asked to 'cancel a subscription,' 5 finished on their own, 1 finished after the moderator gave a hint, and 2 gave up. What is the task success rate?
choices: 8/8, since everyone eventually engaged with the task
6/8, counting the hinted participant as a success
5/8, counting only unaided completions
2/8, counting only the failures
items.explanation: Only unaided completions count as successes — the moment the moderator provides a hint, that attempt no longer measures whether the design communicates on its own, so it's scored as a failure, giving 5 successes out of 8 attempts.
items.reference:
✅ Finished unaided = success
❌ Gave up or got help = failure
🔢 Rate = successes ÷ attempts, per task

Why: it's computed per task, not once for the whole product.

items.prompt: Is task success rate a single number for the whole product, or something else?
choices: A single number computed once for the entire product
A number computed separately per task, since different tasks can have very different success rates
A number that only applies to the very first task in a session
An average of every participant's self-rating
items.explanation: Success rate is task-specific. A product can have a 90% success rate on 'find a product' and a 30% success rate on 'apply a promo code' at the same time — collapsing those into one product-wide number would hide exactly the information a team needs to know what to fix.
items.reference:
✅ Finished unaided = success
❌ Gave up or got help = failure
🔢 Rate = successes ÷ attempts, per task

Why: it's computed per task, not once for the whole product.

items.prompt: What extra information does the think-aloud protocol add beyond a plain pass/fail score?
choices: It makes the test run faster
It reveals why a participant got stuck or confused, not just that they did
It lets participants skip tasks they don't like
It replaces the need for a moderator entirely
items.explanation: A silent failure just tells you something didn't work. Narration ('I'm looking for a way to pay... I don't see one') tells you what the participant expected and where the design failed to meet it — the reasoning a team actually needs to fix the problem.
items.reference:
🗣️ Participant narrates their thoughts while working
🤫 Moderator prompts, never leads
🔍 Turns 'it failed' into 'here's why'

Why: pass/fail alone can't distinguish two very different kinds of failure.

items.prompt: During a think-aloud session, a participant goes quiet for 20 seconds while working. What should the moderator do?
choices: Say nothing and let the silence continue indefinitely
Gently prompt with something neutral like 'what are you thinking right now?'
Tell the participant the correct next step
End the session early since the data is no longer useful
items.explanation: A neutral prompt keeps the narration flowing without leading the participant toward any particular answer. Supplying the next step would contaminate the result the same way a hint does; ending the session throws away a moment that's often the most informative part of it.
items.reference:
🗣️ Participant narrates their thoughts while working
🤫 Moderator prompts, never leads
🔍 Turns 'it failed' into 'here's why'

Why: pass/fail alone can't distinguish two very different kinds of failure.

items.prompt: In a moderated usability test, what is the moderator's main job while a participant is working?
choices: Explain how the design is supposed to work as they go
State the task, then mostly stay quiet and observe, prompting narration if needed
Take over the task once the participant seems stuck
Rate the design themselves in real time
items.explanation: A moderator's restraint is the whole point — the session is measuring whether the design communicates on its own. Explaining, taking over, or rating the design themselves all substitute the moderator's understanding for the design's, which defeats the purpose.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Moderated: someone watches live, in person or remote
📼 Unmoderated: participant works alone, recorded for later review
⚖️ Trade-off: depth of follow-up vs. speed/scale

Why: both formats still require unaided, task-based attempts to count as real usability testing.

items.prompt: What is an unmoderated usability test?
choices: A test where nobody ever reviews what happened
A test where the participant completes tasks alone, often remotely, with the session recorded for the team to review afterward
A test where multiple moderators watch the same participant at once
A test that skips think-aloud narration entirely
items.explanation: Unmoderated just means no one is live-observing during the session — the participant works alone and the interaction (often including their narration) is recorded for the team to review later. It's still a real usability test, just a different format with different trade-offs.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Moderated: someone watches live, in person or remote
📼 Unmoderated: participant works alone, recorded for later review
⚖️ Trade-off: depth of follow-up vs. speed/scale

Why: both formats still require unaided, task-based attempts to count as real usability testing.

items.prompt: What's one real trade-off between moderated and unmoderated testing?
choices: Moderated testing cannot use the think-aloud protocol at all
A live moderator can ask a follow-up question in the moment, while unmoderated testing usually scales to more participants at once but loses that live follow-up
Unmoderated testing never produces a usable task success rate
There is no real difference between the two
items.explanation: The live moderator can chase an interesting moment ('you paused there — what made you hesitate?') that a recording alone can't. Unmoderated tests trade that depth for running more sessions in parallel without needing someone present for each one.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Moderated: someone watches live, in person or remote
📼 Unmoderated: participant works alone, recorded for later review
⚖️ Trade-off: depth of follow-up vs. speed/scale

Why: both formats still require unaided, task-based attempts to count as real usability testing.

items.prompt: A participant says 'I love this design!' but couldn't complete the task without help. Which should a team weigh more heavily?
choices: The stated opinion — if they like it, they'll figure it out with practice
The observed behavior — what people say they'd do and what they actually do reliably diverge
Neither matters until a survey confirms it
Both matter equally and should be averaged into one score
items.explanation: Observed behavior is the whole reason usability testing exists as distinct from a survey. People are often genuinely polite or genuinely unaware of their own struggle — the failed task is the more reliable signal about whether the design actually works.
items.reference:
🗳️ Opinion: what people say
🖱️ Behavior: what people actually do
⚠️ These reliably diverge — trust behavior

Why: a design can be liked and still fail at its actual job.

items.prompt: Why is a team's confidence in a design, formed during internal review, an unreliable predictor of real usability?
choices: Because internal reviewers are always less skilled than real users
Because the team already knows what the design is supposed to mean, so they can't experience the same confusion a first-time user would
Because internal reviews always happen too quickly to matter
Because confidence is never a useful signal for anything
items.explanation: This is the curse of knowledge again: the team's prior knowledge of what everything means makes their own confidence a poor stand-in for a first-time user's experience, regardless of how carefully or quickly the review happened.
items.reference:
🗳️ Opinion: what people say
🖱️ Behavior: what people actually do
⚠️ These reliably diverge — trust behavior

Why: a design can be liked and still fail at its actual job.

items.prompt: What does the widely cited 'five users find most usability problems' idea claim?
choices: Exactly 5 users will always find 100% of a design's problems
A small number of representative participants, around 5, tends to surface roughly 85% of a design's usability problems, with diminishing returns after that
You should never test with more than 5 users
5 users is only useful for testing visual design, not flows
items.explanation: It's a diminishing-returns curve, not a guarantee of completeness or a hard cap. Roughly 85% of problems tend to surface by around 5 representative participants; each additional participant mostly re-finds problems already seen, though testing more can still be worthwhile, especially in later rounds.
items.reference:
📈 Fast gains in the first few participants
📉 Flattens after ~5–10
🔁 Test small, fix, retest — beats one big study

Why: most problems are common enough that a small representative sample reliably catches them.

items.prompt: Given the diminishing-returns curve behind the five-user idea, what's usually the better use of a fixed testing budget?
choices: One large study with 30 participants right before launch
Several small rounds — test ~5, fix what's found, test ~5 more — repeated across the design process
Testing with exactly 1 participant, since any data beats none
Skipping early testing and only testing after the product ships
items.explanation: Because the curve flattens quickly, repeated small rounds catch and fix most problems earlier and cheaper than saving the whole budget for one large study — and each round can test whether the previous round's fix actually worked.
items.reference:
📈 Fast gains in the first few participants
📉 Flattens after ~5–10
🔁 Test small, fix, retest — beats one big study

Why: most problems are common enough that a small representative sample reliably catches them.

items.prompt: Does the five-user idea mean a team can safely skip testing a redesigned flow again after a large change?
choices: Yes, once a design has been tested once, it never needs retesting
No — the curve describes finding problems in a given version; a meaningfully changed flow is effectively a new design and needs its own small round
Yes, because 5 users is a one-time lifetime limit per product
No, because the curve only applies to visual changes, not flow changes
items.explanation: The curve is about how many participants it takes to surface a given version's problems — a substantially redesigned flow can introduce entirely new problems, so it needs its own small test round rather than relying on results from the version it replaced.
items.reference:
📈 Fast gains in the first few participants
📉 Flattens after ~5–10
🔁 Test small, fix, retest — beats one big study

Why: most problems are common enough that a small representative sample reliably catches them.

items.prompt: Why do teams rate the severity of usability problems instead of just listing every failure equally?
choices: Severity ratings are only for legal documentation, not for prioritization
Because a problem blocking most users from finishing a core task deserves more urgency than a cosmetic annoyance, and severity is what encodes that difference
Because every listed problem must be fixed in the exact order it was found
Severity ratings replace the need for task success rate
items.explanation: A flat list treats a typo and a blocked checkout as equally urgent, which they aren't. Severity ranks problems by real impact, so the team fixes what matters most first, rather than whatever's listed first or easiest.
items.reference:
🟢 Cosmetic — noticed, doesn't block
🟡 Minor — slows down, recovers unaided
🟠 Major — blocks most users without help
🔴 Critical — blocks nearly everyone

Why: 'easy to fix' and 'worth fixing first' are different rankings.

items.prompt: Two of six participants hesitated for a few seconds on a button label but all six eventually completed the task unaided. What severity best fits this?
choices: Critical
Major
Minor
Not a usability problem at all, since everyone succeeded
items.explanation: A brief hesitation that participants recover from on their own, without blocking task completion, is a minor problem — real and worth noting, but it doesn't carry the urgency of something that blocks most users.
items.reference:
🟢 Cosmetic — noticed, doesn't block
🟡 Minor — slows down, recovers unaided
🟠 Major — blocks most users without help
🔴 Critical — blocks nearly everyone

Why: 'easy to fix' and 'worth fixing first' are different rankings.

items.prompt: A team has two problems on their list: a critical one blocking most users from checking out, and a cosmetic one that's much faster to fix. Which should they generally prioritize fixing first?
choices: The cosmetic one, since it's quick and clears the list faster
The critical one, even though it takes longer, because severity ranks by real impact, not by effort to fix
Whichever one was reported first in the session notes
Both should always be treated as equally urgent
items.explanation: Severity exists precisely to prevent a team from optimizing for 'easy to fix' by accident. A critical problem blocking a core task outranks a fast, low-impact fix even when the effort comparison points the other way.
items.reference:
🟢 Cosmetic — noticed, doesn't block
🟡 Minor — slows down, recovers unaided
🟠 Major — blocks most users without help
🔴 Critical — blocks nearly everyone

Why: 'easy to fix' and 'worth fixing first' are different rankings.

items.prompt: Which of these is a well-written usability test task?
choices: "Click the gear icon, then tap 'Notifications', then toggle email off"
"Turn off email notifications"
"Tell me what you think of the settings page"
"Explore the app for a few minutes"
items.explanation: A good task states a goal with a clear, observable finish line and doesn't reveal the path — the participant has to find the gear icon and the toggle themselves. The other options either leak the path, ask for opinion instead of behavior, or have no scorable finish line.
items.reference:
🎯 States a goal, not a path
🏁 Has a clear, observable finish line
🚫 Doesn't reveal which icon or label to use

Why: a task that leaks the path or has no finish line can't be scored success/failure.

items.prompt: Why does a task like 'use the search bar to find blue shoes' fail to test what a team usually wants to know?
choices: Because searching is always a bad interaction pattern
Because naming 'the search bar' hands the participant the exact affordance the test was supposed to check they'd discover on their own
Because blue shoes are too specific a product to search for
Because tasks about finding products are never useful to test
items.explanation: Naming the UI element leaks the path. If the real question is whether users can discover how to search for a product, telling them where the search bar is removes exactly the thing being tested — the goal-only version, 'find a pair of blue shoes to buy,' leaves that discovery to the participant.
items.reference:
🎯 States a goal, not a path
🏁 Has a clear, observable finish line
🚫 Doesn't reveal which icon or label to use

Why: a task that leaks the path or has no finish line can't be scored success/failure.

items.prompt: Put these steps in the order they belong in a usability test session: (A) score each attempt success/failure, (B) state the task once, (C) participant works while narrating (think-aloud), (D) moderator prompts narration only if it stops.
choices: A, B, C, D
B, C, D, A
D, B, C, A
C, B, D, A
items.explanation: The task is stated first (B), the participant works while narrating (C), the moderator only steps in to prompt narration if it stops (D), and scoring happens after the attempt concludes (A). Prompting or scoring can't sensibly happen before the task is even stated.
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the task once
2️⃣ Participant works, narrating aloud
3️⃣ Moderator prompts narration only if it stops
4️⃣ Score the attempt after it concludes

Why: scoring has to wait until the attempt is actually over, not happen mid-task.

items.prompt: A moderator scores a participant's attempt as a failure the moment the participant pauses for 15 seconds, before the attempt has actually ended. What's wrong with this?
choices: Nothing — a 15-second pause should always count as failure
Scoring should happen after the attempt concludes (success, failure, or give-up), not mid-task on a pause that the participant might recover from
The moderator should have helped instead of scoring
Pauses should never be recorded at all
items.explanation: A pause isn't the same as failure — participant 3 in this unit's worked example paused for 40 seconds and then succeeded. Scoring has to wait until the attempt genuinely concludes (completion or give-up), not fire early on a moment that might still resolve into a success.
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the task once
2️⃣ Participant works, narrating aloud
3️⃣ Moderator prompts narration only if it stops
4️⃣ Score the attempt after it concludes

Why: scoring has to wait until the attempt is actually over, not happen mid-task.

items.prompt: A participant is visibly struggling and asks, 'Am I doing this right?' What should the moderator say?
choices: "Yes, you're doing great, just click the icon in the corner"
Something neutral like "There's no right or wrong way — just do what feels natural to you"
Stay completely silent and say nothing at all
"No, try a different approach"
items.explanation: A neutral, reassuring redirect keeps the participant working without leaking any information about the design. Confirming, correcting, or giving directions would all contaminate the result; total silence in response to a direct question can also make participants anxious in a way that changes their behavior.
items.reference:
🗣️ State the task once, in plain language
❓ Prompt narration neutrally if it stops
🙅 Never confirm, correct, or point

Why: any hint, however small, shifts the test from measuring the design to measuring the participant's ability to follow instructions.

items.prompt: Why does even a small hint from the moderator ('try tapping that icon') ruin a task's result, rather than just slightly helping it?
choices: Because it makes the session take longer
Because it supplies the exact information the test exists to check whether the design provides on its own — the result stops measuring the design and starts measuring instruction-following
Because participants get offended by hints
It doesn't ruin anything — small hints are fine as long as they're brief
items.explanation: The line isn't about degree — a small hint crosses the same boundary as a large one, because either way the moderator, not the design, is now the source of the missing information. The task can no longer answer the question it was written to answer.
items.reference:
🗣️ State the task once, in plain language
❓ Prompt narration neutrally if it stops
🙅 Never confirm, correct, or point

Why: any hint, however small, shifts the test from measuring the design to measuring the participant's ability to follow instructions.

items.prompt: What is the moderator's role once they've stated the task, according to the session flow in this unit?
choices: Actively guide the participant toward the correct path step by step
Mostly observe and stay quiet, only prompting narration if it stops, without leading toward any answer
Explain the design's intended use before the participant begins
Leave the room entirely so the participant isn't watched
items.explanation: Restraint is the job. Guiding or pre-explaining both substitute the moderator's knowledge for the design's; leaving entirely would prevent the moderator from being able to prompt narration or observe hesitation at all.
items.reference:
🗣️ State the task once, in plain language
❓ Prompt narration neutrally if it stops
🙅 Never confirm, correct, or point

Why: any hint, however small, shifts the test from measuring the design to measuring the participant's ability to follow instructions.

items.prompt: In a session with 7 participants attempting one task, 5 completed it correctly and unaided, and 2 gave up. What's the task success rate?
choices: 5/7, about 71%
2/7, about 29%
5/5, 100%, since only completed attempts count
7/7, 100%, since everyone attempted it
items.explanation: Success rate is unaided completions divided by total attempts: 5 out of 7 participants attempted and completed the task correctly on their own, which is about 71%. The 2 who gave up still count in the denominator — they attempted the task, they just didn't complete it.
items.reference:
🔢 Rate = unaided completions ÷ total attempts
⚠️ A flagged success still counts as a success in the raw rate
🗣️ Narration is what tells you which successes to flag

Why: the raw number and the narration together give the real picture — neither alone is enough.

items.prompt: Of 6 participants attempting a task, 4 finished cleanly and quickly, 1 finished only after 45 seconds of visible hesitation and confused narration, and 1 gave up. What is the strictest, most decision-useful success rate — counting only unflagged, unhesitant completions?
choices: 5/6, about 83%
4/6, about 67%
1/6, about 17%
items.explanation: The bare pass/fail count would be 5/6 (treating the hesitant completion as a plain success), but the flagged-out count that best predicts real-world drop-off is 4/6 — only the clean, unhesitant completions. The hesitant participant's narration signals the same confusion that made the other participant give up entirely.
items.reference:
🔢 Rate = unaided completions ÷ total attempts
⚠️ A flagged success still counts as a success in the raw rate
🗣️ Narration is what tells you which successes to flag

Why: the raw number and the narration together give the real picture — neither alone is enough.

items.prompt: Why does this unit's worked example report two different success-rate numbers (50% and 33%) for the same session?
choices: Because the team made a counting error and one number is simply wrong
Because bare pass/fail and a stricter unflagged count answer different questions — technical completion vs. smooth, friction-free completion
Because the numbers were computed on different days with different participants
Because task success rate is always reported as a range, never a single number
items.explanation: Neither number is a mistake — they answer different questions. Bare pass/fail (50%) answers 'did they technically finish'; the unflagged count (33%) answers the question a launch decision actually depends on: did the design work smoothly enough that a less patient real customer wouldn't have abandoned.
items.reference:
🔢 Rate = unaided completions ÷ total attempts
⚠️ A flagged success still counts as a success in the raw rate
🗣️ Narration is what tells you which successes to flag

Why: the raw number and the narration together give the real picture — neither alone is enough.

items.prompt: A participant narrates: "I'm looking for a way to pay... I don't see one, so I'll try this icon." What does this narration reveal that a bare pass/fail score would not?
choices: Nothing extra — it just confirms the participant eventually acted
That the payment affordance wasn't recognizable as one, which is the specific, actionable cause behind whatever the final outcome was
That the participant disliked the visual design
That the task instructions were unclear
items.explanation: The narration names the exact misreading: the participant couldn't recognize the payment icon as such and had to guess. A bare success/failure score would only tell you the participant eventually did or didn't act, not which specific element failed to communicate and needs fixing.
items.reference:
🗣️ Quote names the specific misreading
🎯 Points at exactly what to fix, not just that something's wrong
🚩 Can flag a technical 'success' as still risky

Why: narration converts an outcome into a diagnosis.

items.prompt: Participant 3 in this unit's worked example said 'That seems like just a summary, not where I'd type something' about the accordion, and then succeeded anyway after 40 seconds. Why does the team still treat her result as a warning sign, not a clean win?
choices: Because 40 seconds is an official failure threshold in every usability test
Because her own words describe the same misreading that caused three other participants to give up entirely — she just happened to push through it
Because she should have asked the moderator for help instead
Because women participants are weighted differently in usability data
items.explanation: Her narration is the giveaway: the confusion she describes (the accordion reading as a summary, not an input location) is identical to what made participants 1, 4, and 6 quit. Her persistence masked the same underlying design failure that produced three outright failures elsewhere in the same session.
items.reference:
🗣️ Quote names the specific misreading
🎯 Points at exactly what to fix, not just that something's wrong
🚩 Can flag a technical 'success' as still risky

Why: narration converts an outcome into a diagnosis.

items.prompt: Two participants both fail the same task. One says nothing while failing; the other narrates 'I thought this button would take me back, not forward.' Which failure gives the team more to act on?
choices: The silent one, since silence means the design is obviously broken
The narrated one — it names a specific, wrong expectation the design created, which points directly at what to change
Neither — both failures are equally uninformative without a survey afterward
They're equally informative, since both simply count as one failure each
items.explanation: Both count equally toward the success rate, but only the narrated failure tells the team why: the button created a wrong directional expectation. The silent failure still counts, but leaves the team guessing at the cause instead of pointing at a specific fix.
items.reference:
🗣️ Quote names the specific misreading
🎯 Points at exactly what to fix, not just that something's wrong
🚩 Can flag a technical 'success' as still risky

Why: narration converts an outcome into a diagnosis.

items.prompt: According to the cumulative-problems-found curve in this unit, roughly what fraction of a design's usability problems does testing around 5 representative participants tend to surface?
choices: About 30%
About 55%
About 85%
100%, with no problems left to find
items.explanation: Around 5 participants, the curve has typically found roughly 85% of a design's usability problems — a large majority, though not all. The remaining problems are found more slowly, with each additional participant mostly re-surfacing ones already seen.
items.reference:
📈 Steep gains for the first few participants
📉 Flattens by ~10–12 participants
👥 Only valid if participants are actually representative

Why: the curve assumes a representative sample — it breaks down otherwise.

items.prompt: A team tested 6 real first-time customers and found 4 major problems. They then tested 6 fellow designers on the same flow and found only 1 minor problem. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: The designers found fewer problems because designers are simply better testers
The designers already carry the curse of knowledge from having built similar products, so they're less likely to hit the same confusion a real first-time customer would
Testing with designers always produces more accurate results than testing with real customers
The flow genuinely improved between the two rounds
items.explanation: This is the same curse of knowledge from L1, now showing up in who gets tested rather than who built the design. Designers' familiarity with common patterns and their own field makes them a non-representative sample — more of the wrong population finds problems faster, not more accurately.
items.reference:
📈 Steep gains for the first few participants
📉 Flattens by ~10–12 participants
👥 Only valid if participants are actually representative

Why: the curve assumes a representative sample — it breaks down otherwise.

items.prompt: A team reports 'our usability test had a 90% success rate' but only counted whether the task technically got completed, ignoring hesitation and moderator hints. What's the risk in trusting this number for a launch decision?
choices: There's no risk — 90% is 90% regardless of how it was counted
It can hide near-failures and moderator-assisted completions inside the count, overstating how ready the design actually is
The risk only applies if fewer than 5 participants were tested
A 90% number is always more trustworthy than a lower one, regardless of method
items.explanation: Exactly like this unit's promo-code example, a generously-counted number can look reassuring while masking real friction — hesitant completions and moderator-assisted ones both inflate a bare pass/fail count above what a stricter, unaided-only count would show.
items.reference:
🎭 A generous count can look better than reality
👥 A non-representative sample inflates confidence too
🔁 Only a fix + retest confirms a problem is actually solved

Why: a number can be technically true and still mislead a launch decision.

items.prompt: After moving the promo code field, a team retests and sees the success rate jump from 33% to 83%. Is that number alone enough to confirm the fix worked well, with nothing left to check?
choices: Yes, a large jump in the number is always sufficient proof on its own
Not entirely — the number shows the fix worked in aggregate, but the think-aloud narration is still the only place a new, different kind of hesitation would show up
No, because success rate can never be trusted after a redesign
Yes, because narration only matters for failures, not successes
items.explanation: The number answers whether the fix worked in aggregate, but it can't by itself distinguish a clean 83% from an 83% hiding new flagged, hesitant successes — exactly the gap between the two counting methods this unit worked through. Checking the narration is still necessary to confirm there's no new, quieter problem underneath the improved number.
items.reference:
🎭 A generous count can look better than reality
👥 A non-representative sample inflates confidence too
🔁 Only a fix + retest confirms a problem is actually solved

Why: a number can be technically true and still mislead a launch decision.

items.prompt: A stakeholder says 'we already tested this once, we don't need to retest after the fix.' What's the strongest counter-argument from this unit's material?
choices: Retesting is never necessary once any usability test has been run
A fix is a hypothesis about what caused the problem — only a retest with fresh participants confirms whether it actually raised success and didn't just move the confusion somewhere else
Retesting is only needed if the first test used fewer than 20 participants
The stakeholder is right, since severity ratings already predict whether a fix will work
items.explanation: A fix is an educated guess about the cause until it's actually observed working. This unit's closing question makes exactly this point: a raised success-rate number is necessary but not sufficient — a retest, including its narration, is what actually confirms the specific confusion is gone.
items.reference:
🎭 A generous count can look better than reality
👥 A non-representative sample inflates confidence too
🔁 Only a fix + retest confirms a problem is actually solved

Why: a number can be technically true and still mislead a launch decision.

items.prompt: Given a task success rate of 33%, a severity of 'blocks most users,' and narration pointing at one specific cause (a collapsed accordion hiding the field), what's the most defensible next step?
choices: Ship as planned, since 33% of users did succeed
Delay launch, move the field to a visible location based on the specific cause identified, and retest before shipping
Remove the promo code feature entirely to avoid the problem
Ask the design team to vote again on whether the placement seems fine
items.explanation: The three pieces of evidence together — a low success rate, high severity, and a specific identified cause — point at a concrete, testable fix. Shipping ignores the data; removing the feature overreacts to a placement problem; another team vote repeats the exact mistake from L1 that started this whole unit.
items.reference:
🔢 Success rate: how big is the problem
🚦 Severity: how urgent is it
🗣️ Narration: what specifically caused it

Why: a launch decision needs all three pieces together, not any one alone.

items.prompt: Why is 'we ran a usability test and the room agreed the fix looks better' not a substitute for retesting with real participants?
choices: Because rooms are never allowed to have opinions about design
Because it repeats the exact original mistake — a team's own confidence, without observed behavior from representative users, was already shown not to predict real usability
Because retesting is only required by policy, not because it adds information
Because a room can never agree on anything about a design
items.explanation: This is the throughline of the whole unit: internal agreement, however sincere, isn't evidence, because the people agreeing already know what the design is supposed to mean. Only observed behavior from representative participants who don't already know that closes the loop.
items.reference:
🔢 Success rate: how big is the problem
🚦 Severity: how urgent is it
🗣️ Narration: what specifically caused it

Why: a launch decision needs all three pieces together, not any one alone.

items.prompt: A different task in the same session had a task success rate of 100% with no flagged successes and no hesitation in the narration. What should the team do with that task?
choices: Redesign it anyway, since every task should be changed after a test
Treat it as evidence the current design works for that task, and prioritize fixing other lower-scoring tasks first
Distrust the 100% result, since no result can ever be fully trusted
Retest it immediately with a completely different set of tasks
items.explanation: A clean 100% with no flags and no hesitation is exactly what a working design looks like in this data — the same three signals (rate, severity, narration) that flagged the promo-code task as a problem here all point the opposite way, toward leaving it alone and focusing effort on the tasks that actually scored poorly.
